Venezuela Lifts Nationwide Curfew as Political Crisis Eases, Business Activity Resumes

Caracas—Business activity across Venezuela began to recover this week after the government lifted a nationwide curfew that had paralyzed commerce for nearly two weeks amid a wave of political unrest. The crisis, triggered by a disputed legislative vote and ensuing mass protests, had forced the closure of factories, ports, and retail centers, dealing a sharp blow to the already-fragile economy.

The unrest, which started in late May, escalated when opposition parties claimed irregularities during parliamentary proceedings and called for nationwide demonstrations. In response, the government imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew, deployed security forces, and restricted intercity transport. The measures halted freight shipments and disrupted supply chains, with industry groups estimating a 40% decline in output across manufacturing and agriculture during the curfew.

Resolution came late Sunday after mediated talks between government officials and opposition leaders, facilitated by representatives from Brazil and the Organization of American States. Both sides agreed to a provisional power-sharing arrangement and scheduled new legislative sessions for next month. President Mateo Ruiz announced the immediate end of the curfew, stating, “We are committed to restoring stability and ensuring that Venezuelans can return to work.”

The National Chamber of Commerce welcomed the agreement. “The resumption of operations is crucial for the recovery of businesses and livelihoods,” said chamber president Luisa Rojas. “We urge all sides to maintain dialogue and avoid further disruptions.”

Analysts cautioned that lingering uncertainty could dampen investment. “While the immediate crisis has passed, Venezuela’s underlying political divisions remain unresolved,” said Javier Ortega, senior economist at LatinFocus Analytics. “Sustained stability will be essential for economic recovery.”

Ports in La Guaira and Maracaibo reopened on Monday, with the first cargo trucks rolling out before dawn. Retailers in Caracas reported brisk activity as supply trucks arrived to restock shelves.
